Water atomization, although not widely used, can produce powders with higher oxygen concentrations and irregular morphologies due to the fast cooling and solidification rates. Gas atomization, on the other hand, is the preferred method, as it yields powders with lower oxygen content, less porosity, and a spherical morphology, which enables easy flow and dense packing. This is particularly beneficial for laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) systems, where optimal spreadability and minimal voids are crucial. Plasma atomization is commonly used for reactive metals and high-purity powders. To ensure the quality of AM 316H metal powder, it is essential to purchase from a manufacturer or vendor who can meet the required powder specifications and characteristics. Furthermore, handling and storage requirements must be strictly followed to control powder properties before and after AM fabrication. This includes guidelines for powder addition and removal, cleaning protocols, humidity-controlled storage, and designated areas for safe storage. Manufacturers often provide specific requirements, and a certification report stating the powder specifications, Lot/Heat ID, and vendor information is also necessary as described in References 4-14. By adhering to these guidelines, the integrity of the metal powder can be maintained, resulting in high-quality AM parts. UNCLASSIFIED AMMT – 316H SS Los Alamos National Laboratory Page 1-2 1.1.1 Pedigree The Kansas City National Security Campus's reference document, 9960010 (U) Selective Laser Melting Powder, provides a comprehensive guide for the characterization of AM powder used in LPBF and selective laser melting (SLM) processes. This document, described in Reference 15, outlines the essential requirements for AM powder, which are further elaborated upon in this section. To ensure the quality and consistency of AM powder, manufacturers and vendors must provide a certification report that includes the specifications and Lot/Heat ID of the powder. This report should contain a full chemical analysis, including electron-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDX) or inductively coupled plasma - mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), Laboratory Equipment Corporation (LECO), mass spectrometry, and general alloy identification per SAE HS-1086 for elemental analysis. This analysis is crucial in determining whether the powder chemistry composition meets the requirements for the intended application. It is strongly recommended that customers perform their own chemical analysis upon receiving the powder to ensure consistent results throughout its shelf life. In addition to chemical analysis, several tests should be performed to evaluate the behavior of the metal powder. These tests include particle size and distribution (PSD) analysis by laser diffraction, Hall Flow, Apparent Density, Tap Density, Skeletal density, Carney Flow, Powder Rheometer, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging to capture the morphology of the metal powder. Equivalent forms of analysis may be accepted. The determination of PSD is particularly important, as it reveals the distribution of powder particles within the accepted average particle size range (~30um). Particles that are too small risk being evaporated by the laser during the build process, causing issues with powder flow and potentially leading to inclusions and voids in the weld pool.
